**(e)** State the posterior predictive distribution of one new observation $X_{\mathrm{new}}$, conditionally independent of the sample given $\mu$.

**(f)** Explain why the posterior predictive variance is larger than the posterior variance of $\mu$.

## Question 5. Normal--inverse-$\chi^2$ regression

Suppose

$$
y\given\beta,\sigma^2,X\sim \Normal_n(X\beta,\sigma^2 I_n),
$$

with prior

$$
\beta\given\sigma^2\sim \Normal_p(\beta_0,\sigma^2\Sigma_0),
\qquad
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{Inv\text{-}\chi^2}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2).
$$

Here $X$ is known, $\Sigma_0$ is positive definite, and $\mu_0,\sigma_0^2>0$. The inverse-$\chi^2$ convention is

$$
\frac{\mu_0\sigma_0^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{\mu_0}.
$$

**(g)** State the full conditional posterior of $\sigma^2\given\beta,y,X$. How does it differ from its marginal posterior?

## Question 14. Inverse-gamma waiting time

The waiting time until the $m$th animal at location $i$ has density

$$
f(x_i\given\theta)
=
\frac{1}{\Gamma(m)\,\theta^{m}}x_i^{m-1}e^{-x_i/\theta},
\quad x_i>0,
$$

so $\theta>0$ is a scale. The prior is

$$
f(\theta)
=
\frac{\beta_0^{\alpha_0}}{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}\theta^{-\alpha_0-1}e^{-\beta_0/\theta},
\quad\alpha_0>0,\ \beta_0>0.
$$

The exam states that the maximum likelihood estimator is $\hat\theta=\bar x/m$.

**(i)** State the prior mean. [1 mark]

**(ii)** Find and identify the posterior distribution of $\theta$. [5 marks]

## Question 15. Battery lifetimes and a Bayes factor

Researchers are attempting to determine the distribution of lifetimes of a type of battery. They have measured the lifetimes (years) of $n$ of these batteries, recorded as $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, which we assume were the result of a random sample and we will assume that the observations could be considered independent and identically distributed. Two models were proposed:

$$
M_1\colon x\sim\Exp(\theta)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
M_2\colon x\sim\Weibull(5,\theta).

$$
f(x)=5\theta x^{4}e^{-\theta x^{5}},
\qquad\text{for }x>0.
$$

**(b)** Find the marginal likelihood under model $M_2$. [3 marks]

## Question 17. Hierarchical Poisson model

Suppose $J$ factories manufacture components. Factory $j$ produces $n_j$ observations of the number of defective components per batch.

Assume

$$
Y_{ij}\given\theta_j\ind\Poisson(\theta_j),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n_j,\quad j=1,\ldots,J.
$$

Here, $\theta_j>0$ represents the expected number of defects per batch in factory $j$.

Rather than modelling the factory rates independently, we assume

$$
\theta_j\given\lambda\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\GammaDist(a,\lambda),
$$

where $a>0$ is known and $\lambda>0$ is an unknown common hyperparameter.

Finally, assign the hyperprior

$$
\lambda\sim\GammaDist(c,d),
$$

where $c,d>0$ are known.

All Gamma distributions use the shape--rate parameterisation:

$$
f(x\given a,b)=\frac{b^{a}}{\Gamma(a)}x^{a-1}e^{-bx},
\qquad x>0.
$$

**(a)** Write down the joint density $p(\Yvec,\thetavec,\lambda)$ up to proportionality in the unknown parameters.

**(b)** Derive the full conditional distribution $p(\theta_j\given\lambda,\Yvec)$ for each factory $j$. Identify its distribution and parameters.

**(c)** Derive the full conditional distribution $p(\lambda\given\thetavec,\Yvec)$. Identify its distribution and parameters.

**(d)** Using your results from (b) and (c), describe a Gibbs sampling algorithm targeting $p(\thetavec,\lambda\given\Yvec)$.

**(e)** Explain how the hierarchical model allows observations from one factory to influence inference about another factory's defect rate.

[Solution](#sol-pois-hier)
:::

::: {#ex-model-selection .exercise}
## Question 18. Bayesian model selection

Suppose $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ are independent observations, with observed data $\yvec=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$. A researcher wishes to compare two competing models.

Under model $M_1$,

$$
Y_i\given\theta,M_1\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\Normal(\theta,1),
$$

where the unknown mean has prior distribution

$$
\theta\given M_1\sim \Normal(0,\tau^2).
$$

Under model $M_2$,

$$
Y_i\given\mu,\sigma^2,M_2\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2),
$$

where the unknown mean and variance have prior distributions

$$
\mu\given\sigma^2,M_2\sim \Normal\Bigl(0,\frac{\sigma^2}{\kappa}\Bigr),
\qquad
\sigma^2\given M_2\sim\InvGamma(\alpha,\beta).
$$

Assume that $n\geq 2$, and $\tau^2,\kappa,\alpha,\beta$ are known positive constants.

The inverse-gamma distribution is parameterised by

$$
f(v;a,b)=\frac{b^{a}}{\Gamma(a)}v^{-a-1}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{b}{v}\Bigr),
\qquad v>0.
$$

Define

$$
\bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_i,
\qquad
S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar y)^{2}.
$$

You may use the identity

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\eta)^{2}=S+n(\bar y-\eta)^{2}
$$

and the result

$$
\int_{0}^{\infty}v^{-a-1}e^{-b/v}\,dv=\frac{\Gamma(a)}{b^{a}},
\qquad a,b>0.
$$

**(a)** Write down the likelihood functions $L_1(\theta;\yvec)$ and $L_2(\mu,\sigma^2;\yvec)$ under models $M_1$ and $M_2$, respectively. [2 marks]

**(b)** Using the prior distribution of $\theta$, derive an expression for the marginal likelihood $p(\yvec\given M_1)$. The derivation should explicitly show the integration over $\theta$, including any completion of the square required. [5 marks]

**(c)** The marginal likelihood under model $M_2$ is given by

$$
p(\yvec\given M_2)
=
\int_0^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
p(\yvec\given\mu,\sigma^2,M_2)\,
p(\mu\given\sigma^2,M_2)\,
p(\sigma^2\given M_2)\,d\mu\,d\sigma^2.
$$

**(i)** Integrate out $\mu$ to obtain an expression for $p(\yvec\given\sigma^2,M_2)$. [4 marks]

**(ii)** Hence integrate out $\sigma^2$ to derive the marginal likelihood $p(\yvec\given M_2)$. [4 marks]

**(d)**

**(i)** Obtain an expression for the Bayes factor

$$
B_{12}=\frac{p(\yvec\given M_1)}{p(\yvec\given M_2)}.
$$

**(ii)** Suppose the prior model probabilities are $P(M_1)=0.25$ and $P(M_2)=0.75$. Express the posterior odds in favour of $M_1$ in terms of $B_{12}$.

[3 marks]

**(e)**

**(i)** Explain why normalising constants that do not depend on the unknown parameters must nevertheless be retained when calculating marginal likelihoods.

**(ii)** State the conditions under which the Bayes factor is well-defined. Explain briefly why replacing the proper parameter priors with unspecified improper priors can cause difficulties in Bayesian model comparison.

[2 marks]

[Solution](#sol-model-selection)
:::
